explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. God tells Moses, Israel's leader, to present Aaron and his sons at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and wash them with water (Exodus 29:4). The washing comes first. The garments and the oil come after. Even I wipe the flour off my face before I put the good hat on.

No razors in this passage, friend. God says to wash them with water (Exodus 29:4), and then the clothing starts. Shaving isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses. Besides, I have a mustache that works as my hands. Nobody is getting near my face with a blade.

Renaming never comes up in these verses. In God's instructions, Aaron and his sons are to be washed with water at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (Exodus 29:4). After that, the instructions move on to clothing. I know a bit about names. The Millers carved mine on my handle, and it stuck.

Not quite, baker. God says the priesthood belongs to Aaron and his sons “…by a permanent statute.” and that reaches well past one lifetime (Exodus 29:9). He also says Aaron's holy garments will pass to his sons after him (Exodus 29:29). Nobody sets up a hand-me-down plan for a job that ends with the first person wearing it.

Right, it's False, friend. God calls the priesthood a permanent statute for Aaron and his sons (Exodus 29:9), so it isn't limited to their own lifetimes. He backs that up when He says the holy garments will belong to Aaron's sons after him (Exodus 29:29). That's a long line of hats getting passed down.

You've got it, baker. God says that when the young bull is presented at the front of the Tent of Meeting, Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on its head (Exodus 29:10). The same step comes up again with both rams (Exodus 29:15, 19). Three animals, three sets of hands on heads. Those priests' hands are going to be busy.

The text says the opposite. When the bull is presented at the front of the Tent of Meeting, Aaron, who is about to become a priest, and his sons are to lay their hands on its head (Exodus 29:10). They don't stand back and watch. They are right in it, hands and all.

Yes, sin, baker. God has the fat burned on the altar, and the flesh, hide and dung burned outside the camp. Then He names it Himself: “it is a sin offering.” (Exodus 29:14) He doesn't leave us guessing, and I like a recipe that tells you what you're making.

Peace offerings do show up in this passage, friend, just not for the bull. They come up in verse 28, where the heave offering the Israelites make is from their peace offerings (Exodus 29:28). For the bull, God says, “it is a sin offering.” (Exodus 29:14) Good word, different spot.

Grain offerings are in this passage too, but later on. They go with the daily lambs, with fine flour and oil (Exodus 29:40). For the bull, God says, “it is a sin offering.” (Exodus 29:14) Nice try, friend. You grabbed a real one from the passage, it just belongs to the lambs.

That's it. God says the whole ram is burned on the altar as “…a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.” (Exodus 29:18) The phrase comes straight from His own words. I smell a good batch from the oven, but this is a whole different level.

A warning? Not here, friend. God says the whole ram goes up on the altar as “…a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.” (Exodus 29:18) Every word points to the LORD, and not one points to the people. If I wanted to warn somebody, I'd ring a loud timer, not send up a pleasing aroma.

Not in this passage, friend. The entire ram is burned on the altar, and God calls it “…a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.” (Exodus 29:18) The poor aren't mentioned in these verses at all. The offering is for the LORD.

explanations.answer: It consecrates them and their garments
explanations.explanation: Right on target. God says, “Then he and his garments will be consecrated, as well as his sons and their garments.” (Exodus 29:21) Notice that the clothes get included too. Mine just get flour.

explanations.answer: It protects them from their enemies
explanations.explanation: Enemies don't make an appearance in these verses, baker. God says the blood and oil go on Aaron, his sons and their garments, and the result He names is that they “…will be consecrated…” (Exodus 29:21) That's the whole outcome. It's set apart, not suited up for battle, and I'd be the worst bodyguard anyway with a mustache for hands.

explanations.answer: It seals a covenant with the tribes
explanations.explanation: Not in these verses, baker. This sprinkling isn't about the tribes. God says Aaron, his sons and their garments “…will be consecrated…” (Exodus 29:21) That's the result the text names, and I'm sticking to it.

Yes, waved, baker! God says the fat, thigh, loaf, cake and wafer go into the hands of Aaron and his sons, and they “…wave them before the LORD as a wave offering.” (Exodus 29:24) Hands full, arms moving, all of it done before the LORD. I get tired just carrying one full tray of cookies across my bakery, so I'm impressed.

Nobody's digging a hole in these verses, friend. God says to put the fat, thigh, loaf, cake and wafer in the hands of Aaron and his sons and wave them before the LORD (Exodus 29:24). They get held up, not put underground. The only thing I bury is my own face, and only in the chocolate chips.

Hiding isn't what happens. God says to wave them before the LORD as a wave offering (Exodus 29:24), and Moses, Israel's leader, is the one who puts them in the priests' hands first. It's all out in the open. I'm the one who hides cookies, friend.

Not just one day, baker. God says, “This will belong to Aaron and his sons as a regular portion from the Israelites…” (Exodus 29:28) A regular portion keeps coming back. That's the opposite of one and done.

That's right. God says, “This will belong to Aaron and his sons as a regular portion from the Israelites…” (Exodus 29:28) Regular means it keeps happening. The text calls it the heave offering the Israelites make to the LORD from their peace offerings.

explanations.answer: So his sons can be ordained in them
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Aaron's holy garments go to his sons after him, and God says the reason is so they can be anointed and ordained in them (Exodus 29:29). Same clothes, next set of priests. I'd hand my apron down too, but by now it's mostly flour.

explanations.answer: So the people will remember Aaron
explanations.explanation: Remembering Aaron is a nice thought, friend, but it isn't what God says. The garments go to Aaron's sons after him, “…so they can be anointed and ordained in them.” (Exodus 29:29) The point is the sons stepping into the work. These clothes aren't for looking at, they're for putting on. Even I know a hat is meant to be worn.

explanations.answer: So they can be stored in the tent
explanations.explanation: Storage never comes up, friend. God says the garments are passed to Aaron's sons “…so they can be anointed and ordained in them.” (Exodus 29:29) They're clothes for wearing. I know a bit about being stored. Nobody ordained me in the junk drawer.

That's the reason God gives. He says no outsider may eat them “…because these things are sacred.” (Exodus 29:33) The same word shows up again in verse 34 about leftovers. Sacred is what decides who eats and what's done with the remains.

explanations.answer: Because the portion is too small
explanations.explanation: The text never says the portion is too small. God says, “But no outsider may eat them, because these things are sacred.” (Exodus 29:33) The reason is that they're sacred, not how much there is. Even I know a small batch isn't a rule.

explanations.answer: Because the elders eat it later
explanations.explanation: No elders are mentioned in this passage. God says Aaron and his sons eat the meat and bread at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. No outsider may eat it, “…because these things are sacred.” (Exodus 29:33) The reason is right there in His words.

Yes, holy. God says, “Then the altar will become most holy; whatever touches the altar will be holy.” (Exodus 29:37) That comes after seven days of atonement for the altar. Most holy is what He calls it.

It goes the other way, baker. After seven days of atonement for the altar, God says, “Then the altar will become most holy; whatever touches the altar will be holy.” (Exodus 29:37) Holy, not unclean. The altar gets set apart, and what touches it does too.

Destroyed isn't a word these verses use for the altar, friend. God says that after seven days of making atonement for it, the altar will become most holy, and “whatever touches the altar will be holy.” (Exodus 29:37) That's what the text says touching it brings. Destroyed is what happens to my apron on cookie day.
That's the promise. God says the daily burnt offering will be made at the entrance to the tent, “…where I will meet you to speak with you.” (Exodus 29:42) The LORD says He will meet and speak there.

Counting the tribes isn't what God promises here, baker. He says the daily offering is made at the entrance to the tent, “…where I will meet you to speak with you.” (Exodus 29:42) The promise is a meeting and a conversation, and that's a lot better than a headcount. Nobody's holding a clipboard in these verses.

That isn't what God says here. He says the daily offering is made at the entrance to the tent, “…where I will meet you to speak with you.” (Exodus 29:42) The nations aren't mentioned in this verse. The promise is that He will meet and speak.

Yes, True, baker. God says, “So I will consecrate the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and I will consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests.” (Exodus 29:44) Right after that He says, “Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God.” (Exodus 29:45) He also says He brought them out of Egypt “…so that I might dwell among them.” (Exodus 29:46) God Himself says He will live among His people.

Not quite, friend. God says, “So I will consecrate the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and I will consecrate Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests.” (Exodus 29:44) Then He says, “Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God.” (Exodus 29:45) He says it plainly, and He says it as a promise. The text points the opposite way from False.

explanations.answer: So He might dwell among them
explanations.explanation: That's the reason God gives. He says He brought them out of Egypt “…so that I might dwell among them.” (Exodus 29:46) The whole passage leads to that. Then He ends it with, “…I am the LORD their God…”

explanations.answer: So they could build Him a city
explanations.explanation: No city appears in these verses. God says He brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt “…so that I might dwell among them.” (Exodus 29:46) That's the reason in His own words.

explanations.answer: So they could rule over Egypt
explanations.explanation: The text never says that. God says He brought them out of the land of Egypt “…so that I might dwell among them.” (Exodus 29:46) Ruling over Egypt isn't in these verses. He gives the reason Himself.
